One dark winter day, a little girl with an unusual face was riding slowly along London's broad streets in a cab beside her father. Yellow fog lay so thick and heavy over the city that the street lamps had been lit, and gaslight shone from the shop windows just as it did at night.

Her feet were tucked beneath her, and she leaned into her father, who had an arm around her. As she watched the people passing outside the window, her wide eyes held a strange, thoughtful look that seemed to belong to someone much older.

On so small a girl's face, that expression was unexpected. It would have looked old even on a twelve-year-old, and Sara Crewe was only seven. Yet she was forever dreaming and thinking curious thoughts; she could not remember ever having lived without wondering about grown-ups and the world they inhabited. To her, it felt as though she had already been alive for a very, very long time.

Just now her thoughts were on the journey she had made from Bombay with her father, Captain Crewe. She remembered the great ship, the Lascars moving silently back and forth across it, and the children playing on the hot deck. She remembered, too, the young officers' wives who would coax her into conversation and laugh at the things she told them.

Above all, she was considering how strange it was to be in India's fierce sunshine at one moment, then out in the middle of the sea, and then riding in an unfamiliar carriage through unfamiliar streets, where daylight was as black as night. It puzzled her so much that she pressed a little nearer to her father.
"Papa," she said, her small voice low and mysterious, almost a whisper. "Papa."
Captain Crewe drew her closer and gazed down at her face. "What is it, darling?" he asked. "What is my Sara thinking about?"
"Is this the place?" whispered Sara, nestling even more closely against him. "Is it, papa?"
"Yes, little Sara. This is it. At last we've arrived." She was only seven, but she could hear the sadness in his words.

It felt like years since he had first begun getting her ready for "the place," as she always called it. Her mother had died at her birth, so Sara had neither known her nor felt her absence. Her father, young and handsome and rich and always petting her, seemed to be her one relation in the whole world. They had always been playmates and loved each other's company. She knew he was rich only because people said so when they supposed she could not hear; she had heard them say, too, that she would be rich herself when she grew up. What being rich really meant, she did not entirely understand. Her home had always been a lovely bungalow, full of servants who made salaams to her, addressed her as "Missee Sahib," and let her have her way about everything. She had toys and pets and an ayah who adored her. Little by little, she had come to understand that rich people had these things. Beyond that, she knew nothing about it.

There had been just one worry in her short life: "the place" where she would have to go one day. India's climate was considered very unhealthy for children, and they were sent away as soon as they could be—usually to school in England. Other children had left before her eyes, and she had listened to their parents discussing the letters that came from them. She had always known that her own turn must come. Sometimes her father's accounts of the voyage and the new country made her want to see them, but the knowledge that he could not stay there with her troubled her.
At five she had asked, "Couldn't you come to that place with me, papa? Couldn't you come to school yourself? I'd help you do your lessons."

"But it won't be such a very long stay, little Sara," he had always assured her. "You'll live in a nice house with lots of other little girls, and you'll all play together. I'll send you plenty of books. You'll grow so quickly that it will hardly seem a year before you're big enough and clever enough to come home and look after papa."

That was a prospect she loved. Managing her father's house, riding beside him, taking her place at the head of his table when he gave dinner parties, talking with him and reading his books—nothing in the world could please her more. If reaching that future meant going away to "the place" in England, then she must resolve to go. Other little girls did not interest her very much, but a good supply of books would comfort her. Books were her greatest delight; indeed, she was constantly making up stories about beautiful things and telling them to herself. Sometimes she had shared them with her father, and he had enjoyed them every bit as much as she had.
"Well, papa," she said gently, "since we have arrived, I suppose we must be resigned."

Her old-fashioned words made him laugh, and he kissed her. In truth, he felt nothing like resigned, although he knew he must not let her see it. His curious little Sara had been wonderful company. He thought how lonely he would be, back in India, walking into his bungalow and knowing that no small figure in a white frock would run forward to welcome him. As the cab turned into the large, gloomy square where their destination stood, he held her tight in both arms.
The house was large, gloomy, and built of brick, just like every other house in the row. Its one distinction was a shining brass plate fixed to the front door, bearing these words in black:
MISS MINCHIN,
Select Seminary for Young Ladies.

"Here we are, Sara," Captain Crewe announced, putting as much cheer into his voice as he could. He lifted her down from the cab; together they climbed the steps and rang. Later Sara often thought how exactly the house resembled Miss Minchin. It was respectable, with good furniture, yet everything was ugly. Even the armchairs seemed to have hard bones inside them. Hardness and polish filled the hall; the red cheeks of the moon face on the tall corner clock looked stern beneath their varnish. They were shown into a drawing room with a square-patterned carpet and square chairs. A weighty marble clock rested on an equally weighty marble mantelpiece.
Settling into one of the unyielding mahogany chairs, Sara gave the room one of her swift, observant glances.
"I don't like it, papa," she told him. "Still, I suppose soldiers don't really LIKE going into battle either—even the brave ones."
At that, Captain Crewe burst out laughing. Young and cheerful himself, he found he could never hear enough of Sara's curious remarks.
"Oh, little Sara," he said, "what will become of me without you to say solemn things? Nobody else can be quite so solemn."
"Then why does something solemn make you laugh like that?" Sara wanted to know.

"Because you're so amusing when you say it," he replied, laughing harder. Then he suddenly gathered her into his arms and kissed her fiercely. His laughter stopped at once, and his eyes looked almost as though they were filling with tears.

At that very moment Miss Minchin came in. Sara thought she was remarkably like the house: tall, dreary, respectable, and ugly. Her eyes were large and cold and fishlike; her smile was large and cold and fishlike too. At the sight of Captain Crewe and Sara, that smile widened enormously. The lady who had recommended her school had told her a great many pleasing things about the young soldier. One of them was that he was wealthy and quite ready to spend a very large sum on his little girl.

Taking Sara's hand and stroking it, she said, "Captain Crewe, it will be a great privilege to care for so beautiful and promising a child. Lady Meredith has spoken of her exceptional intelligence. For a school such as mine, a clever child is a real treasure."
Without moving or speaking, Sara kept her gaze on Miss Minchin's face. As usual, an odd thought was passing through her mind.

"Why is she calling me a beautiful child?" she wondered. "I'm not beautiful in the least. Isobel, Colonel Grange's little girl, is beautiful. Her cheeks are rosy, she has dimples, and her long hair is golden. My hair is short and black, and my eyes are green. Besides, I'm thin, and there's nothing fair about me. Hardly any child I've ever seen is as ugly as I am. She's telling a story to begin with."

But Sara was wrong about her ugliness. She looked nothing like Isobel Grange, the regiment's little beauty, yet she possessed a curious charm all her own. Slim and graceful, she was rather tall for seven, with a small face that was intense and appealing. Her thick hair was truly black and curled only at the ends. Her eyes were admittedly a greenish grey, but they were large, remarkable eyes, fringed with long black lashes. Sara might dislike their colour, but plenty of other people liked it very much. Nevertheless, she remained firmly convinced that she was an ugly little girl; Miss Minchin's compliments did nothing at all to lift her spirits.
"If I called her beautiful, I'd be telling a story," she thought, "and I'd know perfectly well it was a story. I think I'm just as ugly as she is, in my own way. Why would she say such a thing?"
With a longer acquaintance, Sara came to understand Miss Minchin's reason. She found that every father and mother who brought a child to the school heard precisely the same compliment.

Sara remained beside her father, listening to his conversation with Miss Minchin. The seminary had been chosen because Lady Meredith had sent both her little girls there, and Captain Crewe placed great trust in her experience. Sara would be what people called "a parlor boarder," with privileges beyond even those such pupils generally received. She would have a pretty bedroom and a sitting room to herself, a pony and carriage, and a maid in place of the ayah who had looked after her in India.

Holding Sara's hand and patting it, Captain Crewe gave his cheerful laugh. "Her education doesn't worry me at all," he said. "Your difficulty will be stopping her from learning too much, too quickly. She sits for ever with that little nose buried in a book. She doesn't read books, Miss Minchin—she devours them, like a small wolf instead of a little girl. She's always hungry for more, and it's grown-up books she wants: huge, thick volumes in French and German as well as English, history, biography, poets, and everything you can imagine. When she's reading too much, pull her away from it. Send her to ride her pony in the Row, or out to buy herself another doll. She ought to spend more time playing with dolls."
"But papa," Sara explained, "if I bought myself a new doll every few days, I'd soon have more dolls than I could love. They ought to be intimate friends. That's what Emily is going to be to me."
Captain Crewe glanced across at Miss Minchin, and she returned his look.
"And who is Emily?" she asked.
Smiling, Captain Crewe said, "You tell her, Sara."
As Sara replied, her green-grey eyes grew very solemn, and tender too.

"She's a doll I don't have yet," she explained. "Papa is going to buy her for me, and we're going out to find her together. I've named her Emily. When papa has gone away, she'll be my friend. I need her so I can talk to her about him."
Miss Minchin's broad, fishlike smile now took on a positively admiring look.
"Such an original child!" she exclaimed. "Such a darling little creature!"
Drawing Sara against him, Captain Crewe said, "Yes, she is a darling little creature. Please look after her very carefully for me, Miss Minchin."

For several days Sara lived with her father at his hotel; she stayed, in fact, right up until his departure for India. Together they visited one big shop after another and bought an extraordinary number of things—far more, indeed, than she could possibly need. But Captain Crewe was an impulsive, innocent young man. Everything his little girl admired, and everything he admired himself, he wanted her to have. Between them they assembled clothes far too splendid for a seven-year-old. There were velvet dresses edged with expensive fur, dresses of lace, dresses with embroidery, hats trailing great soft ostrich feathers, ermine coats and muffs, and boxes of little gloves, handkerchiefs, and silk stockings in enormous quantities. Behind the counters, the courteous young women whispered together. Surely that odd little girl with the big, serious eyes must be a foreign princess at the very least—perhaps an Indian rajah's little daughter.
Eventually they found Emily. But first there were several toy shops to visit and a great many dolls to inspect before she appeared.

"I want her to look as though she isn't really a doll," Sara explained. "When I talk, I want her to seem as though she LISTENS. What's wrong with dolls, papa"—she tilted her head, considering the matter as she spoke—"what's wrong with them is that they never seem to HEAR." So their search took in dolls both large and small, with blue eyes or black ones, with brown curls or golden plaits, some fully dressed and others without any clothes.

While they were studying an undressed doll, Sara said, "You see, if the one I find hasn't any frocks, we could go to a dressmaker and have them made especially for her. They'll fit so much better if she tries them on."

After several disappointments, they chose to continue on foot, looking through the shop windows while the cab followed behind. They passed two or three shops without going inside at all. Then, as they came towards a shop that was actually quite small, Sara gave a sudden start and caught hold of her father's arm.
"Oh, papa!" she exclaimed. "Emily is there!"
Colour rushed into her cheeks. In her green-grey eyes was the look of someone who had unexpectedly caught sight of a beloved and very familiar friend.
"She's been waiting right there for us!" Sara said. "Let's go inside to her."
"Dear me," Captain Crewe replied, "I almost feel we need somebody to make the introductions."
"You must introduce me, and then I'll introduce you," said Sara. "Though I recognized her as soon as I saw her—so perhaps she recognized me as well."

Perhaps Emily really had recognized her. At any rate, when Sara gathered her into her arms, the doll's eyes looked exceedingly intelligent. She was a big doll, though still small enough to carry comfortably. Her golden-brown hair curled naturally and fell all around her like a cloak. Her eyes were a clear, deep grey-blue, shaded by soft, thick lashes—actual eyelashes, rather than lines painted onto her face.
With Emily on her knee, Sara studied her face. "Of course, papa," she said, "of course this is Emily."

They bought Emily, and actually carried her to a shop selling children's clothes, where she was measured for an outfit every bit as fine as Sara's. She, too, received lace frocks, and others in velvet and muslin, along with hats, coats, lovely lace-edged underclothes, gloves, handkerchiefs, and furs.
"I'd like her always to look like a child whose mother takes good care of her," Sara said. "I'm her mother, even though I mean to make her my companion."

Captain Crewe could have taken enormous pleasure in all that shopping if one unhappy thought had not kept pulling at his heart. Every purchase meant that the parting from his dear, curious little companion was drawing nearer.

In the middle of the night he left his bed and stood gazing down at Sara as she slept, holding Emily in her arms. Sara's black hair lay across the pillow, mingling with Emily's golden-brown curls. Each wore a nightgown with lace ruffles, and each had long eyelashes resting against her cheeks and curling upwards. Emily looked so much like a living child that Captain Crewe was thankful she was there. With a deep sigh, he tugged at his moustache, a boyish look on his face.
"Heigh-ho, little Sara!" he murmured to himself. "I don't think you realize how terribly your daddy is going to miss you."

The following day he brought Sara to Miss Minchin's and left her in her care. His ship was sailing the next morning. He told Miss Minchin that his English affairs were managed by his solicitors, Messrs. Barrow & Skipworth. They would provide any advice she needed and settle whatever bills she sent for Sara. He would send his daughter two letters every week, and she must be allowed any pleasure she requested.
"She's a sensible little thing," he explained, "and nothing she asks for is ever anything it would be unsafe to let her have."
Afterwards he went with Sara to her little sitting room for their farewell. She sat on his knee, gripping his coat lapels in her small hands, and studied his face intently for a long time.
Stroking her hair, he asked, "Are you trying to learn me by heart, little Sara?"
"No," she told him. "I know you by heart already. You're inside my heart." They wrapped their arms around one another and kissed as though neither would ever release the other.

As the cab pulled away, Sara sat on her sitting-room floor, her chin resting on her hands, and watched until it vanished around a corner of the square. Beside her sat Emily, watching it go as well. Miss Minchin sent her sister, Miss Amelia, up to discover what the child was doing. When she arrived, the door would not open.
From inside came a curious, courteous little voice. "I've locked the door," it said. "If you please, I would like to be entirely alone."

Miss Amelia was fat and short and lived in considerable awe of her sister. Of the two she was really the kinder, yet she would never go against Miss Minchin. She returned downstairs with a look of something very like alarm.
"Sister, I've never met such a strange, old-fashioned child," she said. "She's locked herself into her room, and there isn't the tiniest sound coming from her."

"That is a great improvement on kicking and screaming, as some children do," replied Miss Minchin. "I thought one so thoroughly spoiled would throw the entire house into an uproar. If any child has ever had everything her own way, this one has."

"I've been unpacking her trunks and putting away her belongings," Miss Amelia said. "I've never seen anything like those clothes—coats trimmed with sable and ermine, and genuine Valenciennes lace on her underclothes. You've seen a few of her things yourself. What DO you make of them?"

"I consider them quite ridiculous," Miss Minchin said sharply. "Still, they will make a very good appearance at the front of the line when we walk the schoolchildren to church on Sundays. She has been outfitted exactly like a little princess."

Upstairs, behind the locked door, Sara and Emily remained on the floor, staring at the corner where the cab had gone out of sight. Captain Crewe, meanwhile, kept looking back, waving and blowing kisses, as though he could not bring himself to stop.
